info.title: PingCore Discovery API
info.description:
Multi-tenant game-server discovery for studios: heartbeat ingest, a public server list safe to call from shipped game clients, reachability verification, seat reservations/quick-join for the server-browser join path (callable by studio backends OR directly by game clients with a player token), an atomic allocation API for studio backends, and a first-party matchmaker (tickets with relaxed sessions, attribute windows, joinable-session backfill and measured-latency placement) callable by backends or game clients.

**Heartbeat contract:** servers POST /v1/heartbeat every 30 seconds; an entry expires 90 seconds after the last beat (three missed beats delist the server).

**Authentication:** `Authorization: Bearer dsc_...` tokens, issued per Discovery app in the PingCore workspace. Every token carries a scope -- `heartbeat` (ingest: game servers), `allocate` (matchmaking: studio backends), or `both`. A known token on the wrong surface answers 403, an unknown token 401, and a degraded service 503 -- three deliberately distinct signals, so an outage can never look like a revoked credential. Revoking a token takes effect within about a minute (the registry sync interval).

**Player tokens (reservation and ticket routes only):** the four `/v1/apps/{publicId}/...` reservation routes and the three ticket routes also accept a short-lived **player token** (a JWT) straight from the game client -- either **studio-signed** (ES256, minted by your login service with a Signing Key from the workspace) or **anonymous** (HS256, issued here at `POST /v1/apps/{publicId}/player-tokens`). Both are off by default per app. A player sees and releases only its own reservations and tickets, and a player ticket carries floors that stop one client committing a server alone. Player tokens are never accepted anywhere else.

**Locations and latency:** `GET /v1/locations` lists the platform's latency beacons; clients measure them and send the map as `latency` (tickets, quick-join) or `latency.<id>=` (the list), with an optional `maxLatencyMs` ceiling.

**The public list is unauthenticated by design:** the `dscp_` publicId in its URL is not a secret, so game clients (including browser builds -- the endpoint answers `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`) can read their server list directly, with no studio proxy in between.

Platform-internal surfaces are deliberately NOT documented here: the fleet-agent WebSocket (`/v1/agent`, run automatically by the PingCore game supervisor for platform-hosted fleet servers) and the registry-sync endpoint this service pulls from the PingCore platform. Studios never call either.

Guides and integration examples: https://pingcore.io/docs

tags.name: Heartbeat
tags.description: Server ingest: dedicated game servers report themselves every 30 seconds and delist on clean shutdown. Called by game servers, never by game clients.

tags.name: Server List
tags.description: The public, unauthenticated server list game clients read. The publicId in the URL is not a secret -- it is safe to ship inside a game binary.

tags.name: Allocations
tags.description: The atomic server-allocation primitive for matchmakers (first-party or third-party). Studio backends only.

tags.name: Matchmaking Tickets
tags.description: The first-party matchmaker: submit tickets (relaxed sessions, attribute windows, latency placement), poll for a match, cancel -- from a studio backend (`dsc_` allocate token) OR directly from a game client (player token, with tighter bounds). Also the joinable-session publisher (backfill into running sessions) and the read-only matchmaking inspector.

tags.name: Locations
tags.description: The platform's locations and their latency beacons -- public, platform-wide, the ids clients send as `latency` keys.

tags.name: Fleet State
tags.description: Autoscaling and observability reads plus the matchmaker desired-capacity hint.

tags.name: Reservations
tags.description: Seat reservations and quick-join: the player-join path for the server-browser flow, on both server tiers. Callable by studio backends (`dsc_` allocate token) OR directly by game clients (player token).

tags.name: Player Tokens
tags.description: Anonymous player-token issuance: how a game client with no login service gets an identity it can present on the reservation routes. Studio-signed player tokens are minted by the studio itself and need no endpoint here.

post.description:
Call every **30 seconds**. The entry expires **90 seconds** after the last heartbeat, so three missed beats delist the server.

`ip` defaults to the observed source address and `serverId` defaults to `ip:port`, so the minimum viable payload is `{ name, port, players, maxPlayers }`. Send `ip` explicitly only when the source address is wrong (proxied or NAT'd setups).

Advertised IPs must be publicly routable (players could not reach a private address). The TEST-NET documentation ranges (e.g. `203.0.113.x`) are deliberately accepted so copy-pasted smoke tests work.

`meta` is a free-form object of studio-defined keys (map, mode, region, ...) used by the list's `meta.<key>` filters. Its canonical JSON form is capped at 2048 bytes.

The response reports verification state so a studio can self-diagnose: when the app's effective verification mode is `none`, `verified` and `lastProbeError` are `null` (nothing probed the server). Unverified servers keep heartbeating but are hidden from the public list until they pass a probe.

Rate limit: per Discovery app (the whole fleet shares the budget), sized from the app's self-hosted allowance as `max(60, ceil(allowance * 2 * 1.5))` per minute (15,000 at the 5,000 default) unless the deployment sets a service-wide override, plus a per-IP floor. The budget is shared by every Discovery instance; if its counter is unreachable the request answers 503 (retry), never 401.

ip.description: Defaults to the observed source address of this request.

queryPort.description: Probed instead of `port` for `udp-echo` verification when set.

meta.description: Studio-defined filterable fields. Canonical JSON capped at 2048 bytes.

200.description: Heartbeat recorded. `expiresIn` is the TTL; `verified`/`lastProbeError` are `null` when the verification mode is `none`.

expiresIn.description: Seconds until the entry expires without another heartbeat.

verificationMode.description: The mode Discovery actually enforces (open-registration apps are always `udp-echo`).

409.description: A NEW serverId was refused by a ceiling -- machine-readable via `reason`, checked in this order. `self_hosted_cap`: the app's self-hosted allowance, the ceiling on heartbeat-tier game servers (`limit`, 5,000 per app by default; `limit: 0` means self-hosting is disabled for the app). Hosted game servers on PingCore have their own separate ceiling and never count against it, so the message points there or to support. `ip_cap`: the open-registration per-source-IP cap (`limit`). In every case, game servers already live keep heartbeating and refreshing their TTL -- hitting a ceiling never knocks a running fleet offline. (`cap` is no longer returned here: the concurrent-server ceiling bounds hosted game servers only.)

example.message: This source IP already has 10 live servers registered on this app, which is its open-registration per-IP limit. Existing servers keep reporting normally.

delete.summary: Delist a server on clean shutdown
delete.description: Call once on clean shutdown so players stop seeing a dead server immediately instead of waiting out the heartbeat TTL. Idempotent: `removed` is `false` when the entry was already gone.

get.summary: List the live servers of a Discovery app
get.description:
**Public and unauthenticated** -- the `publicId` is not a secret, so this endpoint is safe to call straight from a shipped game client (including browser builds: it answers `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`). Rate-limited per IP.

Results are paged, filtered, and sorted server-side, because a real game browser must never pull a hundred-thousand-server fleet down to the client. `totalServers` counts everything matching the filters BEFORE paging (build page counts from it); `returned` is the size of this page.

### Meta filters

Beyond the fixed parameters, any studio-defined meta key can filter the list:

- `meta.<key>=value` -- case-insensitive exact match, e.g. `meta.map=coastline`.
- `meta.<key>[op]=value` -- typed comparison. Operators: `eq`, `ne`, `gt`, `ge`, `lt`, `le`, `contains`, `in` (comma-separated), e.g. `meta.xp[gt]=1.0`, `meta.name[contains]=coop`, `meta.map[in]=DustII,Airport`. One key can carry several conditions (`meta.xp[gt]=10&meta.xp[lt]=100`), including a bare exact match alongside operators.

Comparison semantics: a comparison is numeric only when BOTH the server's meta value and the query value parse as finite numbers. `gt`/`ge`/`lt`/`le` are numeric-only -- a non-numeric value on either side is a non-match, never a coercion. `ne` is numeric-aware and falls back to case-insensitive string inequality; `eq` (the bare form and `[eq]`) is always a case-insensitive STRING match. That asymmetry is deliberate, so a server reporting `wave=10` matches neither `[eq]=10.0` nor `[ne]=10.0`. Only primitive meta values (string/number/boolean) are comparable.

### Latency

Send your measured round trips per location id from `GET /v1/locations` as `latency.<id>=ms` (integers, at most 32 entries, values up to 10000). `maxLatencyMs` then HIDES every server that does not advertise a `meta.location` you measured at or below the ceiling. `sort=latency` (or `-latency`) orders by your exact measurement, servers with no location or no measurement last in both directions, then by players. `sort=latency` without a map falls back to the default sort; an unknown location key is simply ignored.

### Forward compatibility

**Unknown query parameters (and unrecognised meta operators) are ignored, not rejected.** A client shipped inside a released game build cannot be patched in step with this service, so a newer client's parameters degrade to "no filter" against an older deployment.

When the app's verification mode is not `none`, servers that have not passed a reachability probe are hidden from this list while continuing to heartbeat.

**Draining game servers are hidden.** A hosted game server whose state is `draining` (it is being retired, shut down, restarted after a crash, or is unhealthy) is left out of this list and out of `totalServers`, whatever its `reason`, as soon as it reports the drain (a response already cached under the `Cache-Control` window of this endpoint can still show it for those few seconds). It reappears on its own once it reports any non-draining state, normally `ready`. Quick-join and seat reservations apply the same rule. `GET /v1/apps/{publicId}/fleet-state` still shows it, with its `reason`.

parameters.name: offset
parameters.description: Rows to skip. Page N is `(N - 1) * limit`. Clamped at 0.

parameters.name: hasSlots
parameters.description: `true` keeps servers with room (`players < maxPlayers`); `false` keeps only full servers.

parameters.name: sort
parameters.description: `players`, `name`, `updatedAt`, `latency` (needs `latency.<id>` parameters, else the default), or `meta.<key>`; a leading `-` sorts descending; anything unrecognised falls back to the default. `sort=meta.<key>` is numeric-aware (numbers sort before strings ascending; servers missing the key sort last in both directions). `serverId` always breaks ties, so paging never repeats or skips.

byMetaKey.summary: Descending by a studio-defined meta key

nearest.summary: Lowest measured latency first (with latency.<id> parameters)

parameters.name: latency.<id>
parameters.description: Your measured round trip in ms to location `<id>` (from `GET /v1/locations`), one parameter per location. Non-integer or out-of-range values and entries beyond 32 are ignored.

parameters.name: maxLatencyMs
parameters.description: Hard filter (only with `latency.<id>` parameters): keep servers whose `meta.location` you measured at or below this. Servers without a location or a measurement are excluded.

200.description: One page of matching servers. Cacheable for 5s (matches the internal list cache).

totalServers.description: Matches after filtering, BEFORE paging -- size your pager from this.

post.description:
The platform-owned matchmaking primitive. Never pick a server from the list and hope: allocate, and the service transactionally claims counter capacity on one eligible agent-tier server and returns its connection details. Only platform-hosted (agent-tier) servers are allocatable.

The `context` blob is delivered verbatim to the allocated game server (via the Agones-style `watch/gameserver` stream on platform-hosted servers); its canonical JSON is capped at 8192 bytes.

**Idempotency:** the same `idempotencyKey` replays the original allocation (for 600s) instead of claiming twice, so retries are safe. An allocation not confirmed by a session start within `expiresIn` seconds (60s) is released automatically.

Rate limit: per Discovery app, separate from the heartbeat and reservation budgets (allocations are per-match, not per-player).

claims.description: Counter capacity to claim, e.g. `{ "sessions": 1 }`. Keys match `^[A-Za-z0-9_.-]{1,50}$`.

meta.description: Exact-match meta filters, e.g. `{ "location": "ams" }`. String values only (unlike quick-join, there is no operator form here).

context.description: Opaque blob delivered to the game server. Canonical JSON capped at 8192 bytes.

200.description: Capacity claimed (or the idempotency key replayed the original claim -- see `replayed`).

expiresIn.description: Present on fresh allocations: seconds the claim waits for a session start before auto-release.

409.description: No game server can satisfy this allocation right now. Retryable once capacity exists.

example.message: No game server can satisfy this allocation right now.

503.description: The service is degraded. Either the registry has never loaded or Redis is unreachable (no `reason`, as on every route), or `reason: agent_push_unavailable`: a game server was claimed but Discovery could not notify it (the push failed, or every game server that could be claimed had no connected agent to receive it), so the claim was rolled back before answering. Nothing is left pending, the idempotency key is not stored, and a retry with the same key allocates fresh. Retry with backoff -- **the token is fine**.

example.message: Discovery could not notify the game server; the allocation was rolled back. Retry shortly.

get.description: `ip`/`port` are re-read from the live server record, so they are null if the server has since vanished. `expiresAt` is only set while the allocation is still pending. The record exists only while the allocation is pending or its session runs: treat a 404 after `confirmed` as "ended".

expiresAt.description: Confirm-by deadline while pending, else null.

404.description: Unknown allocation (or unknown Discovery app -- the same 404 either way). Also returned once the session has ENDED: the record is deleted when the game server reports the session over, so a 404 for an allocation you saw `confirmed`, or for the `allocationId` of a `matched` ticket, means the session is over, not an error. (A pending allocation that was never confirmed is released at its `expiresAt` and answers 404 the same way.)

delete.description: Releases the claimed capacity back to the pool. Only pending allocations can be cancelled -- once a session has started (the allocation is confirmed), end the session instead. Releasing a matchmaker BACKFILL allocation also returns its seats to the joinable-session record immediately instead of waiting out the pending TTL.

409.description: The allocation is already confirmed; a running session cannot be cancelled here.

post.description:
Submit a ticket; the service forms matches and allocates them through the same allocation primitive as `POST .../allocations`. Tickets only match with tickets that agree on `queue`, `sessionSize`, and `filters`.

A ticket carries its OWN session requirements -- the service stores no per-app matchmaking config. Idempotent by `ticketId`. A ticket expires after its TTL (300s); expiry IS the queue timeout -- resubmit to requeue.

**Smaller sessions after a wait:** `minSessionSize` + `relaxAfterSeconds` (sent together, 400 `relaxation_incomplete` otherwise). The OLDEST waiting ticket in the group waits `relaxAfterSeconds` for an exact fill before a smaller session of at least `minSessionSize` players is considered; a younger ticket may be pulled into a smaller session before its own delay elapses. A ticket that must never join a partial session omits `minSessionSize`.

**Attribute windows:** `attributes` + `rules` (see the field descriptions). **Backfill:** `joinInProgress: true` makes the ticket eligible to fill a running session that published a joinable record (`POST .../servers/{serverId}/joinable-session`); such a ticket still takes part in normal formation. **Latency:** `latency` + `maxLatencyMs` place the match at the location that minimises the worst member's latency.

Every cross-field 400 carries a machine-readable `reason`. The matchmaker claims `{ sessions: 1 }` per formed match, so fleet servers must advertise a `sessions` counter (the platform default).

**Player token callers (game clients):** the three ticket routes also accept a player token (studio-signed ES256 or anonymous HS256) when the app has that kind switched on under Player Access. A player-token caller is bounded more tightly than a backend, so a single client can never drain one dedicated server per ticket:

- `partySize` at most 8 (400 `party_too_large_for_player`).
- `sessionSize` and `minSessionSize` at least 2 (400 `session_too_small_for_player`).
- `partySize` strictly smaller than both `sessionSize` and `minSessionSize` (400 `party_fills_session_for_player`): at least one OTHER ticket is always needed before a server is committed.
- `relaxAfterSeconds` raised to at least 10 seconds and echoed on the response (a clamp, not a 400).
- `attributes` limited to 0 keys (0 = not accepted: player-supplied ratings are self-asserted, so the operator opts in).
- `context` at most 1024 bytes (400 `context_too_large`).
- at most 1 queued tickets per player (409 `too_many_tickets`); two tickets of one player never share a match.
- `ticketId`, when supplied, matches `^[A-Za-z0-9_.:-]{1,100}$` (400 `invalid_ticket_id`).
- a per-app player budget and a per-player budget on top of the shared per-IP limit (429).

A player sees, polls and cancels ONLY its own tickets (a foreign ticket is the same 404 as an unknown one); posting an existing foreign `ticketId` answers 409 `ticket_id_taken`. The response carries `ownerKind: "player"` and `ownerPlayerId` (the token `sub`), and the game server receives that id as `roster[].playerId` in the delivered allocation context. Poll `GET .../tickets/{ticketId}` every 2 seconds (the match-loop cadence).

requestBody.description: The party and its session requirements. Every field beyond `sessionSize` is optional; a body without the Phase 2 fields behaves exactly as before.

ticketId.description: Idempotency anchor; generated when omitted. Player callers: `^[A-Za-z0-9_.:-]{1,100}$`.

sessionSize.description: Players per formed match. Tickets are combined to EXACTLY fill this unless relaxation applies.

partySize.description: Players on this ticket. Must not exceed `sessionSize` (400 `party_too_large`).

meta.description: Exact-match meta filters. String values only.

context.description: Merged into the allocation context delivered to the game server (per roster entry). Canonical JSON capped at 8192 bytes.

minSessionSize.description: The smallest session this ticket accepts once relaxation is due. Requires `relaxAfterSeconds`; must be <= `sessionSize` and >= `partySize`.

relaxAfterSeconds.description: Seconds the ticket, as the oldest in its group, waits for an exact fill before a smaller session may form around it. Requires `minSessionSize`; must be below the ticket TTL (300s).

attributes.description: Numbers the matcher can compare (e.g. `{ "skill": 1240 }`). Without a rule on a key an attribute is informational and travels on the roster. At most 8 keys for a backend caller.

widenPerSecond.description: Added to the window per second of THIS ticket's wait. Absent = never widens.

maxWiden.description: Cap on the widening. Absent = bounded only by the ticket TTL.

rules.description: Per-attribute windows this ticket imposes on its peers (the key must exist in `attributes`, 400 `rule_without_attribute`). Compatibility is SYMMETRIC: two tickets match only when each ticket's window admits the other, and a rule on a key the peer lacks is a hard mismatch.

latency.description: The client's measured round trip in milliseconds per location id from `GET /v1/locations`. At most 32 entries. Unknown location ids are ignored, never rejected.

maxLatencyMs.description: Hard ceiling: only locations measured at or below it are acceptable, and a location with no measurement is NOT acceptable. Requires `latency` (400 `max_latency_without_map`); a map with every value above the ceiling is refused (400 `no_location_within_ceiling`). Without a ceiling the map is a PREFERENCE: the best-measured locations are tried first and the match still falls back to any ready server.

joinInProgress.description: Opt in to backfill: this ticket may be placed into a running session with open seats (the game server receives a `backfill` push instead of a new `allocation`).

200.description: Queued (or replayed by ticketId). `relaxAfterSeconds` is the value in force (a player caller's value may have been raised to the floor).

expiresIn.description: Seconds until the ticket expires (the queue timeout).

relaxAfterSeconds.description: The value in force (a player caller's value may have been raised to the floor).

400.description:
The payload failed validation. Structural failures (a wrong type, an out-of-range number) carry only a message; every cross-field failure carries a stable `reason`:

- `party_too_large`
- `relaxation_incomplete`
- `min_session_too_large`
- `min_session_below_party`
- `relax_after_too_long`
- `rule_without_attribute`
- `too_many_attributes`
- `too_many_latency_entries`
- `max_latency_without_map`
- `no_location_within_ceiling`
- `context_too_large`
- `party_too_large_for_player` (player tokens only)
- `session_too_small_for_player` (player tokens only)
- `party_fills_session_for_player` (player tokens only)
- `invalid_ticket_id` (player tokens only)

example.message: minSessionSize and relaxAfterSeconds must be sent together: the floor is the smallest session you accept, the delay is how long the oldest ticket waits for an exact fill first.

409.description:
Two conflicts, told apart by `reason`, both player tokens only:

- `too_many_tickets` -- this player already holds `limit` queued tickets (`active` is the current count). Cancel one or wait for it to match or expire.
- `ticket_id_taken` -- the `ticketId` is already held by a ticket this player does not own, so it cannot be replayed. Choose a fresh id (a UUID) or omit `ticketId`.

example.message: You already have 1 ticket in the queue. Cancel it with DELETE /v1/apps/{publicId}/tickets/{ticketId} or wait for it to match or expire, then retry.

get.description: Poll until `status` is `matched`, then read `ip`/`port` (and `allocationId`/`serverId`). `backfill` says whether the ticket joined a running session; `location` is the placement location when latency constrained it. An expired ticket answers 404 -- resubmit to requeue. A `matched` ticket stays readable for the rest of its TTL, which can outlive the allocation it points at: once the game server reports the session ended, `GET .../allocations/{allocationId}` answers 404, which means the session is over, not an error. A player sees only its own tickets (a foreign ticket is the same 404). Poll every 2 seconds.

200.description: The ticket. Allocation fields are null until matched.

404.description: Unknown ticket -- it may simply have expired, or (for a player token) it belongs to another player: deliberately the same 404. Also the unknown-Discovery-app answer. Resubmit to requeue.

delete.description: Cancels a still-queued ticket. A player cancels only its own (a foreign ticket is the same 404 as an unknown one); a backend cancels anything in its app.

404.description: Unknown ticket -- it may have expired, or (for a player token) it belongs to another player: the same 404. Also the unknown-Discovery-app answer.

409.description: The ticket already matched; release the allocation instead.

post.description:
Tell the matchmaker that a RUNNING session on this server has open seats, so `joinInProgress` tickets in `queue` can be placed into it (backfill). The seats are consumed through the same allocation primitive as a new match, with `kind: backfill`: the game server receives a `backfill` push (never a new `allocation`), claiming `{ players: seats }` when it advertises a `players` counter.

`openSeats` is what you PUBLISH and is never decremented here. Seats the matchmaker has already sold but the game has not yet counted live in a separate pending-joiner ledger, so a republish never re-sells them; reservation holds on the same server are subtracted too. Republish every `ttlSeconds / 2` and immediately when seats change, with `openSeats = maxPlayers - connected - expectedJoiners` -- **`expectedJoiners` MUST include every roster entry returned by the joinable-session GET (or `GET /allocations/{id}`) that has not yet connected.**

Withdraw the record with `DELETE .../joinable-session` the moment your session ends. Discovery also refuses backfills to a server that is no longer `in_session`, but the withdraw is what stops players being matched into a lobby that is closing.

A join-in-progress game needs a `players` counter capacity of at least its match size. When the server advertises a `players` counter, a publish whose `openSeats` exceed that counter's free capacity (`capacity - count`) is refused with 409 `seats_exceed_capacity` and nothing is stored: every backfilled player claims one `players` seat, so those seats could never fill. A hosted server publishing over its agent socket gets the same refusal as a `joinableRejected` frame. A backfill that fails later anyway shows its reason on the matchmaking inspector (`lastBackfillRefusal`).

Only agent-tier servers are allocatable, so only platform-hosted servers can be backfilled: `allocatable: false` tells a heartbeat-tier (or idle) publisher why nothing will fill. **Until the supervisor update ships, backfill on hosted servers is only safe for games that admit any connecting player; games that authorise from the roster must not publish joinable records.**

requestBody.description: The open seats and which tickets qualify. Republishing replaces the record.

queue.description: The ticket queue this session accepts.

openSeats.description: Seats currently free for joiners (the PUBLISHED figure). Capped at 1000 (400 `too_many_open_seats`).

sessionSize.description: When set, only tickets asking for exactly this sessionSize qualify.

attributes.description: Session-side numbers a ticket's `rules` are checked against, one-sidedly (the record has no rules of its own).

sessionId.description: Your own session/allocation id, opaque, echoed as `sessionId` in the backfill context.

ttlSeconds.description: Record lifetime. Capped at 300 (400 `ttl_too_long`). Republish every ttlSeconds / 2.

200.description: Published (or republished). `allocatable` is whether the server is live, agent-tier and in_session RIGHT NOW; the record is stored regardless.

400.description: The payload failed validation. Cap failures carry a `reason`: `too_many_open_seats`, `ttl_too_long`, `too_many_attributes`.

404.description: Unknown server (not live in this app, or a malformed id) -- or unknown Discovery app.

409.description: `seats_exceed_capacity`: `openSeats` exceed the free capacity of the game server's `players` counter, so the seats could never fill. Nothing was stored (an earlier record stays as it was). Raise the counter capacity to at least the match size, or publish no more seats than are free.

freeCapacity.description: capacity - count of the players counter, floored at 0.

get.summary: Read a joinable session and its unconfirmed backfills
get.description:
The HTTP publisher's roster feed: the record with its EFFECTIVE open seats (published minus pending joiners minus reservation holds) and every backfill matched to this server that the game has not yet confirmed, each with its roster.

A backfill is visible here for at most 60 seconds after it is matched (the pending-joiner entry expires on that clock whether or not anyone read it). Poll at least every 30 seconds while a record is live, or persist allocationIds from your own `GET /allocations` polling.

A LIVE server with no record answers 200 with `record: null` and `backfills: []` (a publisher polling after its own withdraw must not see an error). A server that is not live in this app answers 404 `Unknown server.` -- the record cannot outlive the server it describes.

200.description: The record (null when the live server has none) and every not-yet-confirmed backfill, oldest first.

effectiveOpenSeats.description: openSeats minus unexpired pending joiners minus unexpired reservation holds, floored at 0.

expiresAt.description: When this entry leaves the feed if never confirmed.

playerId.description: The player token `sub` for a player-submitted ticket, null for a backend ticket.

404.description: Unknown server: the serverId fails the pattern OR the server is not live in this app (a stale record for a dead server is never shown) -- or unknown Discovery app. A live server with no record is a 200 with `record: null`.

delete.description: Idempotent: always 200, whether or not a record existed. Call it the moment the session ends. Backfills already matched but not yet confirmed stay accounted until they confirm or time out.

get.summary: Inspect the matchmaking queues and joinable sessions
get.description:
Per-queue depth, join-in-progress counts, oldest wait, per-location demand, and every live joinable session with its effective seats and delivery state. This is what the PingCore workspace's Matchmaking card reads.

`truncated` is true when the queued count hit the loop's per-tick cap (500), so the inspector shows exactly what the matcher considers.

**Read scope is per app:** on a PRIVATE app any active token of the app reads (every token there is a secret); on an OPEN-registration app only an allocate-scope token reads, because an open app's heartbeat token ships inside the game and must not expose the studio's queue (403 `reason: scope`).

Rate limited per Discovery app on its own budget (120 per window), separate from allocations. Every response carries `generatedAt` (epoch ms). Nothing is written by these routes.

openSeats.description: Sum of the PUBLISHED openSeats across the queue's joinable sessions.

queuedByLocation.description: Location id -> tickets that accept it (a ceiling-constrained ticket counts once under EVERY location it accepts); the `*` key, always last, counts tickets with no latency ceiling. A queue whose demand sits in a zone with no ready servers is a fleet capacity gap, not a matchmaking fault.

effectiveOpenSeats.description: openSeats minus pending joiners minus held reservation seats, floored at 0.

pendingJoiners.description: Seats matched but not yet confirmed by the game.

allocatable.description: Live, agent-tier and in_session right now.

deliveredToAgent.description: null = no backfill pushed yet; true = every pending backfill is fresh and the server has a live agent connection; false = a backfill older than two loop intervals is still unconfirmed (an un-upgraded supervisor ignoring the push) or the server has no agent at all (an HTTP-only publisher).

lastBackfillRefusal.description: Why the last backfill onto this record did not go through, or null when none has failed since it was published (a republish clears it). The matchmaker retries every tick, so a reason that stays here names a configuration problem: `counter_full` = the game server's `players` counter has less free capacity than the seats being filled (a join-in-progress game needs a `players` capacity of at least its match size); `server_not_in_session` = the server left in_session; `seats_unavailable` = pending joiners or seat reservations already hold the seats; `no_capacity` = the allocation claim refused the server for another reason; `agent_push_unavailable` = the backfill frame could not be delivered (see `/health`).

get.summary: List the platform locations and their latency beacons
get.description:
**Public and unauthenticated** (wildcard CORS, cacheable for 5 minutes): the platform's locations, identical for every app. `id` is byte-identical to the `meta.location` value platform-hosted servers advertise, so it is the key to use in `latency` maps on tickets, quick-join and the list.

An id names a latency ZONE, not a city: its `pingUrl` beacon may sit in a different city than some of the servers that advertise it, so a measurement is accurate to the zone. Measure by opening a WebSocket to `pingUrl`, sending the text frame `ping`, and timing the `pong`; take the median of five samples. Locations with `pingUrl: null` cannot be measured but are listed so the id still resolves on a running server; `enabled` says whether the platform is currently taking new deployments there.

Sorted by `id`. Answers 503 until the service has loaded its locations from the platform.

pingUrl.description: WebSocket latency beacon; null when the zone has none.

503.description: The locations have not been loaded yet: `Discovery has not loaded its locations yet. Retry shortly.` Retry shortly.

example.message: Discovery has not loaded its locations yet. Retry shortly.

Each `servers[]` entry is an ADDITIVE contract -- fields are only ever added, never removed or renamed. `verified` / `lastProbeError` report the reachability probe on both tiers (see `FleetServerEntry`); the example is a hosted game server that is still listed although its UDP game port did not answer the probe.

desiredReadyServersByLocation.description: The same hint split by location (a location id from GET /v1/locations -> ready game servers wanted there), written by the first-party matchmaker on the ticks it writes the hint: each match that found no game server is counted under the location it would be placed in -- the best-ranked location its tickets accept (their latency ceilings, a pinned filters.meta.location) or, without a ceiling, the best one they measured, INCLUDING a location no live game server advertises yet (that is where capacity is missing). A match with no latency map and no pinned location counts in desiredReadyServers only, so the values sum to at most desiredReadyServers; the rest is location-agnostic demand. Locations with no demand are omitted (an empty object when all demand is location-agnostic or zero). Null exactly when desiredReadyServers is null. A studio hint written with PUT desired-capacity has no split: that write clears it.

put.description:
A TTL'd demand hint (expires after 600s): how many READY servers your matchmaker wants available. When your matchmaker goes quiet, the fleet falls back to its configured ready buffer rather than pinning stale demand forever.

Studios running their own matchmaker write this; the first-party ticket matchmaker maintains it automatically while its queue is non-empty, together with a per-location split (`desiredReadyServersByLocation` on matchmaking-stats). A value written here carries no split and clears the first-party one.

expiresIn.description: Seconds until the hint expires (goes quiet).

post.description:
Issues a short-lived **anonymous player token** for this app -- no login, no studio backend. The game client presents it as `Authorization: Bearer <token>` on the reservation routes (reserve, quick-join, get, release) and sees only its own reservations.

Unauthenticated by design (the `dscp_` publicId is not a secret), and safe to call from a browser build (`Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`). Only available when **anonymous player tokens** are switched on for the app under Player Access in the PingCore workspace. Available on **open-registration** apps as well as private ones -- issuance and verification depend only on the publicId and this service's own signing secret, never on the app's `dsc_` token, so an app whose server token is public loses nothing here.

**Lifetime:** 21600 seconds. Reuse the token for the whole session -- issuance is rate-limited per address far more tightly than the reservation routes, and every issued token is a fresh identity against the per-player reservation cap.

**Limits:** anonymous identities bound a token and an address, not a person. A player may hold at most 2 active reservations, reserve at most 8 seats per reservation, and attach at most 1024 bytes of context. Studio-signed tokens are the accountability upgrade when you need to ban or trace a player.

Any request body is ignored.

200.description: Token issued. `expiresAt` is epoch milliseconds; `expiresIn` is seconds from now.

token.description: The compact JWT (`alg: HS256`, `iss: pingcore-discovery`). Treat it as a bearer secret for its lifetime.

playerId.description: The token `sub`: `anon:` followed by a UUID. Appears as `ownerPlayerId` on reservations this token creates.

403.description: Anonymous player tokens are switched off for this app (`reason: anonymous_tokens_disabled`). Turn them on under Player Access on the app's page in the PingCore workspace (allow up to 60 seconds to apply).

example.message: Anonymous player tokens are turned off for this app. Turn them on under Player Access on the app's page in the PingCore workspace (allow up to 60 seconds to apply).

429.description: Too many token requests from this address. Reuse the token you already have.

example.message: Too many player-token requests from this address. Reuse the token you already have; tokens are valid for several hours.

503.description: The registry has never loaded (retry), or this PingCore Discovery deployment has no anonymous-token secret configured (`reason: anonymous_tokens_unavailable`). The second is a platform-side deployment configuration gap, NOT the app's Player Access switch (that one answers 403 `anonymous_tokens_disabled`): nothing in the workspace fixes it, and `GET /health` reports it as `playerAuth.anonymousAvailable: false`. Contact PingCore support; studio-signed player tokens keep working.

post.summary: Reserve seats on a chosen server
post.description:
Hold seats on a CHOSEN server before the player connects, so ten players seeing "1 slot free" cannot all pile in. Works on both server tiers with zero server-side configuration.

Availability is `maxPlayers - players - active reserved seats`. **The hold TTL is the release mechanism** (default 60s, max 300s) -- there is no join detection and no mandatory confirmation protocol; `DELETE` just releases sooner.

**Idempotency:** the optional `reservationId` is the idempotency anchor -- the same id replays the original outcome (for 600s) instead of holding seats twice. Omit it and every call is a fresh hold.

A serverId the public list would HIDE answers the same 404 as one that does not exist -- reservations never confirm hidden servers.

**Hosted game servers:** a hold placed on a PingCore-hosted game server is pushed to that game server over its platform connection (a `reservation` frame with the hold, `playerIds`, `context`, `expiresAt` and owner fields), and again whenever it reconnects; releasing it early or letting it lapse sends `reservationReleased`. Self-hosted game servers check holds with `GET /v1/reservations/verify/{reservationId}?serverId=...` instead.

Rate limit: per Discovery app, a separate budget from allocations (reservations are per-player-join, an order of magnitude chattier than per-match allocations).

**Player tokens (game clients):** this route also accepts a player token (studio-signed ES256 or anonymous HS256) in place of the `dsc_` token, when the app has that kind switched on under Player Access. A player-token caller is bounded more tightly than a backend:

- `seats` at most 8 per reservation and `context` at most 1024 bytes (400 otherwise).
- at most 2 active reservations per player (409 `too_many_reservations`).
- a per-app player budget and a per-player budget on top of the shared per-IP limit (429).

The response carries `ownerKind: "player"` and `ownerPlayerId` (the token `sub`). A player can later inspect and release ONLY its own reservations.

requestBody.description: The hold. Every field is optional (one seat, default TTL), except that `playerIds`, when present, must match `seats`.

reservationId.description: Idempotency anchor. Omit for a fresh hold every call.

seats.description: Seats to hold -- the whole party fits or nothing is held. Capped at 100.

playerIds.description: Opaque per-seat identifiers. When present, must have exactly `seats` entries.

ttlSeconds.description: Hold length. Expiry releases the seats.

context.description: Opaque blob delivered to the reserved game server (in its `reservation` frame when hosted, on a verify that names the matching `serverId` when self-hosted; never to an open app's shipped heartbeat token). Canonical JSON capped at 8192 bytes.

200.description: Seats held (or replayed -- same shape, see `replayed`; `expiresIn` is always the seconds actually remaining).

404.description: Unknown server -- deliberately the SAME 404 whether the serverId does not exist, is hidden from the public list, or is malformed (and the same one an unknown Discovery app gets). The reservation surface never confirms servers the list hides.

409.description:
Three distinct conflicts, told apart by `reason`:

- `no_seats` -- not enough free seats; the whole party fits or nothing is held. `available` reports the seats currently free. Retryable once seats open up.
- `too_many_reservations` -- player tokens only: this player already holds `limit` active reservations (`active` is the current count). Release one or wait for a hold to expire.
- `reservation_id_taken` -- player tokens only: the `reservationId` is already held by a reservation this player does not own, so it cannot be replayed. Choose a fresh id (a UUID) and retry.

example.message: Not enough free seats on this server.

post.summary: Reserve seats on the best visible server
post.description:
"Just get me into a game": filters the VISIBLE servers exactly like the public list, picks the most populated server that still fits the party (players want lively servers -- the opposite of allocation's drain-friendly packing), and reserves atomically, falling to the next candidate if a claim races out.

`filters.meta` speaks the list's own operator model in JSON form: a scalar is an exact match (`{ "map": "Chernarus" }` mirrors `?meta.map=Chernarus`), an object is `{ operator: value }` (`{ "xp": { "gt": 10 } }` mirrors `?meta.xp[gt]=10`). Unknown operators are ignored, never rejected -- the list's forward-compatibility rule, kept identical here.

**Idempotency:** `idempotencyKey` is required and replays like allocations. For a player-token caller the key is scoped to that player, so two players reusing the same key never see each other's reservation.

**Hosted game servers:** a hold placed on a PingCore-hosted game server is pushed to that game server over its platform connection (a `reservation` frame with the hold, `playerIds`, `context`, `expiresAt` and owner fields), and again whenever it reconnects; releasing it early or letting it lapse sends `reservationReleased`. Self-hosted game servers check holds with `GET /v1/reservations/verify/{reservationId}?serverId=...` instead.

**Latency:** send your measured round trips per location id (from `GET /v1/locations`) as `latency`; candidates are then ranked by 25 ms bucket ascending (servers you have not measured last) before the population tiebreak, and `maxLatencyMs` HIDES servers without a measured location at or below it. Without a map the ranking is unchanged. Both callers get the same 400s: `too_many_latency_entries` (more than 32 entries) and `max_latency_without_map`.

**Player tokens (game clients):** this route also accepts a player token (studio-signed ES256 or anonymous HS256) in place of the `dsc_` token, when the app has that kind switched on under Player Access. A player-token caller is bounded more tightly than a backend:

- `seats` at most 8 per reservation and `context` at most 1024 bytes (400 otherwise).
- at most 2 active reservations per player (409 `too_many_reservations`).
- a per-app player budget and a per-player budget on top of the shared per-IP limit (429).

The response carries `ownerKind: "player"` and `ownerPlayerId` (the token `sub`). A player can later inspect and release ONLY its own reservations.

seats.description: Seats to hold -- the whole party fits or nothing is held. Capped at 100.

playerIds.description: Opaque per-seat identifiers. When present, must have exactly `seats` entries.

oneOf.description: Operator form, e.g. `{ "gt": 10 }`. Operators: `eq`, `ne`, `gt`, `ge`, `lt`, `le`, `contains`, `in`. Unknown operator keys are ignored, never rejected.

meta.description: The list's operator model in JSON form: scalar = exact match, object = `{ operator: value }` (e.g. `{ "xp": { "gt": 10 } }`).

context.description: Opaque blob delivered to the reserved game server (in its `reservation` frame when hosted, on a verify that names the matching `serverId` when self-hosted; never to an open app's shipped heartbeat token). Canonical JSON capped at 8192 bytes.

latency.description: The client's measured round trip in milliseconds per location id from `GET /v1/locations`. At most 32 entries. Unknown location ids are ignored, never rejected.

maxLatencyMs.description: Hard ceiling on quick-join: servers whose location you did not measure at or below it are excluded. Requires `latency`.

200.description: Seats held on the chosen server -- read `serverId`/`ip`/`port` for where to connect.

400.description: The payload failed validation. The latency bounds carry a `reason`: `too_many_latency_entries`, `max_latency_without_map`.

409.description:
Three conflicts, told apart by `reason`:
- `no_seats` -- no visible server can seat this party right now (retryable).
- `too_many_reservations` -- player tokens only: this player already holds `limit` active reservations (`active` is the current count). Release one or wait for a hold to expire.
- `reservation_id_taken` -- the `idempotencyKey` resolved to a hold this caller may not see (another player's), so it cannot be replayed. Retry with a fresh key (a UUID).

example.message: No visible server can seat this party right now.

get.description:
Returns the reservation while its hold is live. A reservation's public lifecycle is exactly its seat hold: expired and released both read as the same 404.

**Player tokens:** a player-token caller sees only reservations it owns (`ownerKind: "player"` with its own `ownerPlayerId`). Another player's or a backend's reservation reads as the same 404 as an unknown one -- the surface never confirms a reservation the caller may not see.

404.description: Unknown reservation -- it may simply have expired or been released, or (player tokens) belong to someone else (or unknown Discovery app).

delete.description:
Idempotent by contract: releasing an unknown, expired, or already-released reservation is still a 200. TTL expiry releases the seats anyway -- DELETE just does it sooner.

On a PingCore-hosted game server, the release that actually ends a live hold is also pushed to that game server (a `reservationReleased` frame with `reason: "released"` over its platform connection; a hold that lapses gets `reason: "expired"`), so the game server stops expecting the player.

**Player tokens:** a player releases only its own reservations. Releasing another player's or a backend's reservation is a no-op that still answers 200 (the same shape as unknown), so the response never confirms a foreign reservation exists.

200.description: Released (or there was nothing left to release).

get.summary: Verify a join (called by the game server)
get.description:
How a SELF-HOSTED (heartbeat) game server authorizes a join: the player presents their `reservationId` in the connect handshake, and the game server checks it here with its OWN heartbeat credential (the verifier IS the game server), naming itself with `serverId` and the joining player with `playerId`.

Returns **200 with a `valid` flag for every reservation state** -- unknown, expired, released, and even malformed ids all read `{ "valid": false }`, so a game server has exactly one code path; only a transport or storage failure produces an error status.

**On an OPEN-registration app the heartbeat token ships inside the game, so it gets the verdict only.** Anyone can extract that token, so a call with it is answered exactly `{ "valid": true }` or `{ "valid": false }`: never a `reason`, never `playerIds`, `context`, `seats`, `serverId`, `expiresAt` or the owner fields, so it cannot learn where a hold sits or who is in it. It must send both `serverId` and `playerId`; a call that leaves either out reads `{ "valid": false }` (Discovery logs it for the operator). Discovery then decides the seat itself:

- a hold with `playerIds` admits exactly the listed players;
- a hold without `playerIds` (unnamed seats) made with a player token admits its owner (the token `sub`, studio-signed or `anon:`) on every call, and the owner occupies one of the `seats`; every other player takes one of the remaining seats, first come, first served;
- a hold without `playerIds` made by your backend seats any `seats` players, first come, first served;
- a player Discovery already admitted is admitted again on every later verify of that hold (a reconnect), and two players racing for the last seat cannot both get it. A release or expiry of the hold clears the admissions.

**An admission holds its seat until the hold is released or expires.** Leaving your game server does not give the seat back, and anyone who holds the `reservationId` can claim a free seat of an unnamed hold without ever joining (the shipped token is in every copy of the game, and your `serverId` is public on the list). Use a named hold (`playerIds`) whenever you know the party; leave `playerIds` out only for a party you cannot name in advance.

**`valid: true` does not authenticate the player.** It says the `playerId` your game server sent may take a seat, not that the connecting client is that player: authenticate the `playerId` yourself (for example from the player's studio-signed token) and refuse a second live connection with the same id. In particular the owner's id is admitted even after the hold is full.

So pass the id the player reserved with (their token `sub` for a player-made hold), and post `playerIds` when only named players may use a hold. The `reservationId` is still what a player must know to take a free seat, so post unguessable ids (quick-join ids are random; a `reservationId` you choose on create should be a UUID, never a sequence or a player name).

**Every other heartbeat-capable token** (a private app's heartbeat token, or a `both`-scope token from a server you control) gets the detailed answer. A live hold on a DIFFERENT game server of the app reads `{ "valid": false, "reason": "wrong_server" }` with no details; with `playerId`, a live hold here that does not list the player reads `{ "valid": false, "reason": "not_in_reservation" }` with no details (a hold without `playerIds` names every player, and no seat is counted: read `seats` and count yourself). A valid answer carries the hold's details, `context` included when you sent `serverId`.

Calling without `serverId` is **deprecated** (removed in 1.6.0) for these tokens and still answered until then -- the details of the hold for whichever game server holds it, WITHOUT `context` -- with an RFC 9745 `Deprecation: @1790640000` response header (the deprecation date, 2026-09-29); compare `serverId` against your own yourself until you send it. **Until 1.6.0 the `wrong_server` answer is therefore not a secrecy boundary for these tokens:** a caller that got `wrong_server` can repeat the call WITHOUT `serverId` and read the hold details (`serverId`, `seats`, `playerIds`, `ownerKind`, `ownerPlayerId`; never `context`). That second read goes away when the deprecated form is removed. A token that ships in the game is never offered the deprecated form.

PingCore-hosted game servers do not call this route: each hold on a hosted game server is pushed to it over its platform connection (a `reservation` frame when placed, `reservationReleased` when released or expired, and every live hold again whenever the game server reconnects), and the game server verifies players locally.

Verification is optional by design: a game server that ignores reservations still benefits, because the browser stops overcommitting it.

This route accepts ONLY a heartbeat-capable credential -- never a player token. In the detailed answer, `ownerKind` / `ownerPlayerId` tell you who reserved: with studio-signed player tokens, compare `ownerPlayerId` against the identity of the connecting player.

parameters.name: serverId
parameters.description: The own serverId of the CALLING game server (the one it heartbeats with). Required with a token that ships in the game (an open app's heartbeat token; without it the answer is `{ "valid": false }`). For every other token optional until 1.6.0 only: omitting it is deprecated, withholds `context`, and sets `Deprecation: @1790640000` (RFC 9745) on the response.

parameters.name: playerId
parameters.description: The joining player: an id in the hold's `playerIds`, or for a player-made hold the `sub` of the token it was made with. Required with a token that ships in the game (without it the answer is `{ "valid": false }`), optional otherwise. An empty, over-long or repeated value names nobody.

200.description: The verdict. A token that ships in the game gets exactly `{ "valid": true }` or `{ "valid": false }`. Every other token gets `reason` with some `valid: false` answers, and the detail fields with `valid: true`.

reason.description: Never sent to a token that ships in the game. Otherwise present only with `valid: false`, and then no other field is returned: `wrong_server`, the hold is live but on another game server; `not_in_reservation`, the hold is live on your game server but its `playerIds` do not list `playerId`. An unknown, expired, released or malformed hold has no `reason`.

serverId.description: Equals the `serverId` you sent (when you sent one).

context.description: The hold's `context`, only with a matching `serverId`: `null` when the hold has none, absent (not null) in the deprecated no-`serverId` form. Like every detail field, never sent to a token that ships in the game.

get.description: Redis reachability, registry freshness (age of the last successful registry sync), the heartbeat-tier probe backlog (`probes.pending`; hosted game servers are probed from a separate pool not counted here), and the agent push path (`agentPush`). Answers 503 when Redis is unreachable, when no registry has ever loaded, when the last successful sync is stale, or when the agent push path is failing (the pub/sub preflight failed, or the most recent agent channel subscribe or allocation push failed; a later success or a passing preflight clears it). `degraded` names every failing component, and is empty when healthy. Never authenticated and never rate-limited into failure -- operators check it precisely when things are broken. Note: this endpoint does NOT use the standard success envelope; `error` mirrors overall health. Two informational blocks never degrade it: `agent.connections` (hosted game servers whose agent WebSocket on THIS instance has sent its hello; zero while a fleet is running means the front door is dropping the WebSocket upgrade) and `playerAuth` (whether this deployment can issue and verify anonymous player tokens: `anonymousAvailable: false` means every anonymous token answers 503 `anonymous_tokens_unavailable`, a platform-side deployment configuration gap that no app setting fixes; studio-signed tokens are always available).

degraded.description: The failing components, empty when healthy.

agentPush.description: The Redis pub/sub path that carries allocation and backfill frames to agents. Counters are per process since boot. `lastFailure` carries the stage and time only; the Redis error text is in the service log.

preflight.description: A PUBLISH + SUBSCRIBE/UNSUBSCRIBE probe on a channel in the agent push namespace, run at boot and on every registry sync interval.

subscribed.description: Successful agent push channel subscribes since boot (every connect and reconnect counts; not a gauge of current connections).

subscribeFailed.description: Agent push channel subscribes that failed; each closed its agent socket with 1011 `push channel unavailable`.

publishFailed.description: Allocation pushes that failed after the claim; each claim was rolled back and answered 503 `agent_push_unavailable`.

agent.description: The agent WebSocket ingest on this instance. Informational: never degrades health.

connections.description: Hosted game servers with an agent connection on this instance that has sent its hello (a gauge, unlike agentPush.subscribed; a socket still waiting for its hello is not counted). An aggregate across apps, never per tenant. Zero while a hosted fleet is running means agents cannot connect: check that the front door passes the WebSocket upgrade to /v1/agent.

playerAuth.description: Which player-token kinds this deployment can issue and verify. Informational: never degrades health. A capability only, never key material.

anonymousAvailable.description: False when this deployment has no anonymous-token secret: every anonymous issue and every anonymous (HS256) token then answers 503 anonymous_tokens_unavailable, whatever the app Player Access switch says. A platform-side deployment configuration gap; contact PingCore support.

signedAvailable.description: Always true: studio-signed tokens are verified with the public keys each app registers, and need nothing from the deployment.

anonymousAvailable.description: False when this deployment has no anonymous-token secret: every anonymous issue and every anonymous (HS256) token then answers 503 anonymous_tokens_unavailable, whatever the app Player Access switch says. A platform-side deployment configuration gap; contact PingCore support.

signedAvailable.description: Always true: studio-signed tokens are verified with the public keys each app registers, and need nothing from the deployment.

get.description: The machine-readable specification for the studio-facing surface documented here. Public and cacheable.

heartbeatToken.description: A `dsc_` Discovery token with the **heartbeat** (or **both**) scope, issued on the Discovery app page in the PingCore workspace. This is the credential held by game servers themselves.

allocateToken.description: A `dsc_` Discovery token with the **allocate** (or **both**) scope. Held by studio backends (matchmakers, join services) -- never shipped inside a game client.

playerToken.description:
A short-lived **player token** (a compact JWT) presented by the game CLIENT itself on the reservation routes. Two kinds, each switched on per app under Player Access on the app's page in the PingCore workspace (both off by default):

- **Studio-signed** (`alg: ES256`): minted by the studio's own login service with the private half of a Signing Key generated in the workspace; Discovery verifies against the public half. Claims: `aud` = the app publicId, `sub` = your player id (1-128 chars of `A-Za-z0-9_.:@-`, must NOT start with `anon:`), `exp`, `iat`; optional `kid` header selects the key.
- **Anonymous** (`alg: HS256`): issued by Discovery at `POST /v1/apps/{publicId}/player-tokens`, no login required. `sub` is `anon:<uuid>`.

A player sees and releases ONLY its own reservations and tickets. Player tokens are never accepted on heartbeat, allocation, joinable-session, matchmaking-inspector, fleet-state or verify routes. Rejections carry a machine-readable `reason` (see the 401 responses).

Player tokens are accepted on **open-registration** apps exactly as on private ones: the player path binds the caller to the app through the public `publicId` and the token's own signature, never through the app's `dsc_` token, so it never relied on that token being secret.

OwnerKind.description: Who holds the reservation or ticket: `backend` for a `dsc_` allocate-token caller, `player` for a player-token caller. Additive since API 1.1.0 (tickets since 1.2.0); records created before player tokens existed read as `backend`.

OwnerPlayerId.description: The owning player's id (the player token `sub`) when `ownerKind` is `player`; `null` for backend-held reservations. Game servers using studio-signed tokens compare this against the connecting player on verify.

reason.description: 401 reasons. `signed_tokens_disabled` / `anonymous_tokens_disabled` are 403s and `anonymous_tokens_unavailable` is a 503 -- see those responses.

PublicServer.description: A server as game clients see it. Deliberately narrower than the ingest shape: verification bookkeeping is a studio diagnostic, not something players see.

FleetServerEntry.description: One live server in the fleet-state projection. This shape is an ADDITIVE contract: fields are only ever added, never removed or renamed.

counters.description: Agent-observed counters; null for heartbeat-tier servers.

pendingClaims.description: Not-yet-confirmed allocation claims per counter, service-owned.

verified.description: The reachability probe verdict, on BOTH tiers. `pending` until the first probe lands (a hosted game server is first probed within about 30 s of connecting, a self-hosted one on its first heartbeat), then `verified` or `unverified`, re-probed every VERIFY_REPROBE_SECONDS (default 300 s) with the app's verification mode. Null when the app's verification mode is `none` (nothing probes the server). On a hosted (agent-tier) game server it is a diagnostic only: an `unverified` hosted game server stays on the public list, because the platform allocated its endpoint and health-checks its process. On a self-hosted game server `unverified` hides it from the list.

lastProbeError.description: Why the last probe failed (for example `No UDP echo response before timeout`); null after a passing probe, before the first probe, and when the mode is `none`.

reason.description: Why the agent says it is in this state. Null for heartbeat-tier servers and for any agent that does not send one. Informational: nothing in Discovery branches on it.

FleetStateCounts.description: Totals per lifecycle state across the fleet.

expiresIn.description: Seconds remaining on the hold. Always recomputed, so a replay reports the seconds actually left rather than the original TTL.

replayed.description: True when an idempotency anchor replayed the original outcome.

PublicId.name: publicId
PublicId.description: The app public ID (`dscp_...`). Not a secret -- safe to ship in a game client. On authenticated routes it must additionally match the bearer token's app, or the request answers the same 404 an unknown app gets.

ServerIdPath.name: serverId
ServerIdPath.description: The server identifier. The default form is `ip:port` (IPv6 bracketed), which contains a colon -- URL-encode it.

ValidationError.description: The payload failed validation. Fix the payload; do not retry unchanged.

Unauthorized.description: Unknown or malformed bearer token. Check the token.

Forbidden.description: The token is KNOWN but not usable here: the app is disabled, the token is revoked, or the token lacks the scope this endpoint requires. Distinct from 401 (unknown token) and 503 (degraded service) by design -- do not rotate credentials on a 403.

UnknownApp.description: Unknown Discovery app. An unknown publicId and a DISABLED app deliberately return the same 404, so the API never confirms a disabled app exists. On authenticated routes this is also the answer when the publicId does not match the token's app.

RateLimited.description: Rate limited. Back off and retry (`Retry-After` gives the seconds). Authenticated budgets are per Discovery app -- traffic from one app never spends the budget of another -- and are shared by every Discovery instance; per-IP limits apply only to unauthenticated routes and as a pre-auth floor.

PlayerOrBackendUnauthorized.description:
Unknown or malformed bearer token. For a `dsc_` token: check the token. For a player token the body carries a machine-readable `reason` (`malformed_token`, `unsupported_alg`, `no_signing_keys`, `unknown_kid`, `bad_signature`, `missing_claim`, `invalid_sub`, `invalid_claims`, `audience_mismatch`, `token_expired`, `token_not_yet_valid`, `lifetime_too_long`) and an actionable message.

With no bearer at all: `Missing bearer token. Send an allocate-scope Discovery token (dsc_...) from your backend, or a player token (JWT) from the game client.`

example.message: The token audience does not match this app. Set aud to "dscp_...".

PlayerOrBackendForbidden.description: The credential is KNOWN but not usable here. For a `dsc_` token: the app is disabled, the token is revoked, or it lacks the allocate scope. For a player token: the token kind is switched off for this app -- `reason` is `signed_tokens_disabled` (ES256) or `anonymous_tokens_disabled` (HS256); turn it on under Player Access in the PingCore workspace (allow up to 60 seconds to apply).

example.message: Studio-signed player tokens are turned off for this app. Turn them on under Player Access on the app's page in the PingCore workspace (allow up to 60 seconds to apply).

PlayerOrBackendDegraded.description: The service is degraded: the registry has never loaded, Redis is unreachable, or (anonymous player tokens only, `reason: anonymous_tokens_unavailable`) this PingCore Discovery deployment has no anonymous-token secret configured. That last case is a platform-side deployment configuration gap, NOT the app's Player Access switch: nothing in the workspace fixes it, retrying does not help until PingCore configures the deployment, and `GET /health` reports it as `playerAuth.anonymousAvailable: false`. Use a studio-signed player token or a backend allocate token meanwhile. **The credential is fine**.

Degraded.description: The service is degraded (the registry has never loaded, or Redis is unreachable -- including the shared rate-limit counter on a write, which fails closed with `Rate limiting is temporarily unavailable. Retry shortly.`). Retry -- **the token is fine**. A degraded service never answers 401, so an outage can never look like a revoked credential.
